## Abstract
If single crossing is violated, global incentive compatibility constraints have to be taken into account. This paper studies monotone solutions in a screening model that allows a one-time violation of single crossing.
The results show that local and non-local incentive constraints distort the solution in opposite directions.  Furthermore, the well-known “no distortion at the top” property does not necessarily hold. The results show that the decision can even be distorted above first best for all types. Sufficient conditions for existence, (strict) monotonicity and continuity of the solution are presented. A new necessary condition satisfied by such solutions is found.
## Introduction
The main technical difference is that incentive constraints in the current paper can bind between types choosing different contracts from the menu. Qualitatively, the solution in Araujo and Moreira (2010) features either a discontinuity or a bunching interval. Furthermore, there is a no distortion at the top result, so the type with the highest first-best decision^2 will be assigned this very decision under the optimal mechanism.

Aloisio Araujo, Carolina Parra, Sergei Vieira

August 19, 2026·econ.TH·arXiv:2608.19474

## Abstract

We study one-dimensional screening when the Spence-Mirrlees condition fails along a monotone dividing curve, on which all types value marginal output equally. A single ratio, marginal distortion over marginal rent, governs the problem. When the relaxed solution stays in the positive region, non-decreasing optima in the positive single-crossing region are continuous if the ratio increases in the decision. When it crosses a flat curve and marginal rents are separable, every continuous contract is improved by a jump. When it crosses a strictly monotone curve, a contract that pools and jumps continues along the mirror of the pool if the ratio does not increase along it. Optimality among all implementable allocations, deterministic or random, is proved by a measure on the binding constraints whose weights are the same ratio; with constant curvatures and no crossing, it is also necessary. As applications, we solve problems of procurement and nonlinear pricing.

## Abstract
The single crossing assumption simplifies the analysis of screening models as local incentive compatibility becomes sufficient for global incentive compatibility. If single crossing is violated, global incentive compatibility constraints have to be taken into account. This paper studies monotone solutions in a model where single crossing is violated. Vieira§ This version: October 2026 Abstract We study one-dimensional screening when the Spence–Mirrlees condition fails along a monotone dividing curve, on which all types value marginal out- put equally. A single ratio, marginal distortion over marginal rent, governs the problem. When the relaxed solution stays in the positive region, non-decreasing optima in the positive single-crossing region are continuous if the ratio increases in the decision. # Adverse selection without single crossing: monotone solutions 

Christoph Schottmüller 

> Department of Economics, University of Copenhagen, Øster Farimagsgade 5, building 26, 1353 Copenhagen K, Denmark

Abstract 

The single-crossing assumption simplifies the analysis of screening models as local incentive compatibility becomes sufficient for global incentive compatibility. If single crossing is violated, global incentive compati-bility constraints have to be taken into account. This paper studies monotone solutions in a screening model that allows a one-time violation of single crossing. The results show that local and non-local incentive constraints distort the solution in opposite directions. Depending on the application, the type represents the production technology of a firm in models of regulation (Baron and Myerson, 1982, Laffont and Tirole, 1987), the productivity of a worker in an employment relationship (Guasch and Weiss, 1981) or the willingness to pay for a product in models of monopoly pricing (Mussa and Rosen, 1978).
In all these applications, the authors assume single crossing (SC)1: types can be ordered according to their marginal rate of substitution between money and the decision, e.g. the quantity purchased in a monopoly pricing problem or the quantity produced in a regulation setup. With the commonly used quasilinear preferences, SC is equivalent to a type ordering according to marginal utilities/costs; e.g. a higher type has a higher marginal utility at every consumption level. The private information of an agent is then his eagerness to consume more.
While SC is a technically convenient assumption, we can think of many unobserved differences other than eagerness/efficiency. Some people are very eager at first but quickly get saturated while others have more steady preferences. Compare, for example, single-person households with families. At low quantities, single persons might have a higher marginal willingness to pay for standard groceries because of a higher income per household member. At high quantities, however, families will have the higher marginal willingness to pay as single persons are already saturated. This violates SC: household types cannot be ordered according to their marginal willingness to pay.

### Daniel Gottlieb†and Humberto Moreira‡ This version: May 31, 2024

#### Abstract This paper examines how market power affects coverage in markets with adverse

**selection. We show that market power decreases coverage for individuals who are less willing to pay for insurance but increases coverage for those with a higher willingness to pay. Under weak conditions, a monopolist always excludes a positive mass of customers, whereas competitive firms do not. However, to avoid cream skimming, competitive firms provide less coverage than a monopolist for consumers who are willing to pay more. ## Lumpiness and the Standard Picture

Economists often employ a convenient set of assumptions regarding the goods that individuals care about and the form of individuals’ preferences for these goods. For short, call this set of assumptions “the Standard Picture.” (1) Individuals’ preferences are “outcome-oriented,” in the sense that each individual cares about her own holdings of various goods—goods such as income, health, leisure, or environmental quality—rather than about the relation between her holdings and others’, or about the processes by which her holdings were produced. If there are *M* goods, an individual’s preference structure takes the form of a ranking of possible *M*-dimensional bundles of the goods. (2) An individual’s holding of each good is measured by a real number (for short, the good is numerically “quantifiable”). (3) Each good is infinitely divisible. That is, the range of possible holdings of the good corresponds to some interval of real numbers. (For example, an individual’s annual income might be any nonnegative real number. An individual’s daily leisure might be any real number between 0 and 24 hours, inclusive.) (4) An individual’s preferences with respect to bundles of goods can be represented by a real-valued utility function that is continuous, and that is monotonically increasing in each good. Roughly, a continuous function is one that doesn’t “jump.” A function is monotonically increasing in a given input if its value increases as the input value increases, holding constant the value of the other inputs.

## Overview

The screening model (self-selection) analyzes how an uninformed party designs a menu of contracts, prices, or product versions so that informed agents reveal their private information through their choices. Instead of directly observing “type” (for example, riskiness in insurance, willingness to pay in pricing, ability in taxation, or cost in procurement), the principal induces *self-selection* by offering options that make each type choose the one intended for it. Screening matters because it underpins second-degree price discrimination, insurance design, credit terms, and regulatory contracts—core levers for monetization, risk management, and policy.

## Origins and Credit

Foundational contributions include George Akerlof’s adverse selection (1970s) as the motivating asymmetry; Michael Spence’s signaling (1973) as the informed side’s counterpart; and Joseph Stiglitz and Michael Rothschild’s competitive insurance model (1976), which characterized separating equilibria. James Mirrlees (1971) formalized optimal income taxation as a screening problem. Sanford Grossman, Oliver Hart, and Jean-Jacques Laffont with David Martimort advanced mechanism design foundations. In pricing, Stephen Mussa and Sherwin Rosen (1978) and Eric Maskin and John Riley (1984) developed nonlinear (menu) pricing under private information. There are two sides: a principal (insurer, seller, regulator) and agents (customers, firms, taxpayers) who privately know their type (risk, valuation, cost, ability). In games of mechanism design, agents send messages `M` in a game environment `g`. **Mechanism design** (sometimes **implementation theory** or **institution design**) is a branch of economics and game theory. It studies how to construct rules—called mechanisms or institutions—that produce good outcomes according to some predefined metric, even when the designer does not know the players' true preferences or what information they have. Mechanism design thus focuses on the study of solution concepts for a class of private-information games.

Mechanism design has broad applications, including traditional domains of economics such as market design, but also political science (through voting theory). It is a foundational component in the operation of the internet, being used in networked systems (such as inter-domain routing), e-commerce, and advertisement auctions by Facebook and Google.

Because it starts with the end of the game (a particular result), then works backwards to find a game that implements it, it is sometimes described as **reverse game theory**. Leonid Hurwicz explains that "in a design problem, the goal function is the main given, while the mechanism is the unknown. Therefore, the design problem is the inverse of traditional economic theory, which is typically devoted to the analysis of the performance of a given mechanism."

The 2007 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded to Leonid Hurwicz, Eric Maskin, and Roger Myerson "for having laid the foundations of mechanism design theory." The related works of William Vickrey that established the field earned him the 1996 Nobel prize.

webiq.snippet: 该论文研究了一类存在“最小有效规模”（minimum efficient scale）的筛选问题，其中 Spence–Mirrlees 条件（单调交叉条件，Single-Crossing Condition）沿一个单调的“分界曲线”（dividing curve）失效。### 核心方法与结论  论文提出了一个关于最优契约形状的“三歧定理”（trichotomy），取决于分界曲线与松弛解（relaxed solution）的几何关系：  1. **无交叉（No crossing）**：当松弛解完全处于单调交叉区域的一侧时，最优契约必定是**连续的**。作者通过引入关于原函数（primitives）的“失真-租金比”（distortion–rent ratio）单调性假设（Assumption H），证明了连续性是必须满足的。 2. **平坦分界曲线（Flat dividing curve）**：当分界曲线呈水平状时，**跳跃（jump）是不可避免的**。任何连续契约在分界线处都会被跳跃式契约所主导，代理人在跳跃点处被分配一个产出区间。 3. **严格单调分界曲线（Strictly monotone crossing）**：这是最复杂的情况，跳跃表现为一种“选择”。契约在跳跃后会跟随一条“镜像曲线”（mirror curve），直到松弛解再次追上。
